oneLine: Paul introduces his gospel to a divided church he has never met, showing that the God of Israel has kept his promises in the Messiah and now makes Jews and Gentiles one family that must welcome each other.

author.name: Paul (with Tertius as scribe)
author.who: A Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, trained as a Pharisee, who after meeting the risen Jesus saw himself as Israel's Messiah's envoy to the nations. By the time of Romans he had spent about twenty years planting churches from Syria to the Adriatic coast.
author.howWeKnow: The letter names Paul as sender (Rom 1:1) and Tertius as the man who physically wrote it (Rom 16:22). Its style, themes and travel plans match Galatians and the Corinthian letters, and no serious scholar doubts it. It was used by Clement of Rome in the 90s and was in every early collection of Paul's letters.

writtenFrom.note: Paul is about to take the money collected from Greek churches to Jerusalem (Rom 15:25-26). He commends Phoebe of Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, who probably carried the letter (Rom 16:1-2), and he is staying with Gaius (Rom 16:23), likely the Gaius he baptised in Corinth (1 Cor 1:14). This fits the three-month stay in Greece of Acts 20:2-3.

writtenTo.who: Several house churches in Rome, a mixed body of Jewish and Gentile believers, with Gentiles probably the majority by now
writtenTo.situation: Paul had not founded or visited these churches. Romans 16 greets around 26 people and at least three household gatherings, so the 'church in Rome' was a network rather than one building. Jewish believers who had been expelled under Claudius had returned, and disputes about food and holy days were straining relationships between groups (Rom 14:1-6). Paul also needed Rome as a base and supporter for a new mission to Spain (Rom 15:24).

worldEvents.event: Claudius expels Jews (or some Jews) from Rome after disturbances 'at the instigation of Chrestus', as Suetonius puts it; Priscilla and Aquila leave for Corinth (Acts 18:2). The year comes from the later writer Orosius and is debated.
Claudius dies and Nero becomes emperor; the expulsion lapses and Jews, including Jewish believers, return to Rome.
Paul writes Romans from Corinth before sailing for Jerusalem with the collection.
Public complaints in Rome about abusive indirect taxes, recorded by Tacitus, Annals 13.50-51; some link this to Paul's advice on paying taxes and dues (Rom 13:6-7).
Great Fire of Rome; Nero blames and executes Christians, some of whom may have heard this letter read.

backdrop:
Rome had a large Jewish community, perhaps tens of thousands strong, spread across several synagogues in the districts across the Tiber. The message about Jesus probably arrived there through Jewish travellers and pilgrims (Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome at Pentecost), so the first Roman believers met within or alongside the synagogues. Nobody knows who founded the church; Paul says he did not, and no early source credibly names Peter as founder at this date.

The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting 'at the instigation of Chrestus' (Claudius 25.4). Many historians think 'Chrestus' is a garbled form of 'Christus', meaning arguments in the synagogues about Jesus the Messiah. Acts confirms that Priscilla and Aquila had to leave Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2). If Jewish believers were away for some years, the house churches would have become largely Gentile in leadership and habits. When the Jewish believers came back after 54, they found churches that ate differently and kept different days. This reconstruction (popularised by Wolfgang Wiefel and Peter Lampe) is widely used but not certain; it explains Romans 14-15 and Paul's warning to Gentiles not to look down on Israel (Rom 11:17-21) well.

Paul writes at a turning point. He considers his work in the eastern Mediterranean done (Rom 15:19-23). He is about to deliver money from Gentile churches to the poor believers in Jerusalem, a gift he sees as proof that Jews and Gentiles are one family (Rom 15:26-27), and he fears both unbelievers in Judea and the Jerusalem church's reception (Rom 15:31). Then he wants to go west to Spain, a land with few Jews and no synagogues to start from. Romans is therefore part theology, part peace-making, and part mission support letter: Paul lays out what he preaches so that a church which has heard rumours about him (Rom 3:8) can trust him and stand with him.

culture.explain: There were no church buildings. Believers met in homes or in the back rooms of workshops, perhaps 20 to 40 people each. Romans greets 'the church in their house' of Priscilla and Aquila and other groups named by household (Rom 16:5, Rom 16:10-11, Rom 16:14-15). Different houses could easily develop different practices, which is part of why Paul pleads for welcome.

Phoebe is called a diakonos (servant or minister) of the church at Cenchreae and a prostatis, a word used for a patron or benefactor who uses wealth and status to support others. Letters were carried and often read aloud and explained by the courier, so Phoebe was probably the first person to perform and interpret Romans in Rome.

In a society that ranked people by honour, a crucified Messiah was shameful. Paul's 'I am not ashamed of the gospel' is a public claim to honour in a message the world despised. He also reverses status games: no one can boast before God, Jew or Greek (Rom 3:27), and believers are to outdo one another in showing honour (Rom 12:10).

Jews kept kosher food laws and the Sabbath as signs of belonging to God's covenant. Some believers (Paul calls them 'weak in faith') ate only vegetables, probably to avoid meat that was not kosher or had been offered to idols, and kept special days. Others ate anything. Paul agrees in principle with the 'strong' but tells them not to wreck a brother's faith over dinner.

Roman adoption gave an outsider, often an adult, the full name, rights and inheritance of a new father, and cancelled old debts. Paul uses it both for Gentiles brought into God's family and for Israel's own calling as God's son.

Roman believers lived in the capital of an empire that called Caesar lord and saviour. Paul's teaching on governing authorities comes right after commands not to take revenge, and the empire's sword was a daily reality for a small, suspected minority.

jewishLens:
Romans is a Jewish letter about the faithfulness of Israel's God. Its first sentence calls the gospel something God 'promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy scriptures' about a son of David (Rom 1:2-3), and it quotes the Jewish Scriptures more than any other letter of Paul, over fifty times. The key phrase 'the righteousness of God' (Rom 1:17, Rom 3:21) would remind a Jewish hearer of the Psalms and Isaiah, where God's righteousness is his covenant faithfulness: his commitment to put things right and rescue his people (Ps 98:2-3, Isa 46:13). So the question underneath the letter is not only 'how can I be saved?' but 'has God been faithful to what he promised Abraham, that all nations would be blessed through his family?' (Rom 4:16-18).

That is why chapters 9-11 are not a detour. If most of Israel has not accepted Jesus as Messiah, has God's word failed (Rom 9:6)? Paul, writing with grief for his own people (Rom 9:2-3), answers no: Israel's 'stumbling' is temporary and serves the inclusion of the nations, Gentiles are wild branches grafted into Israel's olive tree, not a replacement tree, and 'all Israel will be saved' (Rom 11:17-26). The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (Rom 11:29).

Scholars read this Jewishness in different ways. Traditional Reformed and Lutheran readers (Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner) see Paul showing that Jews too need to be justified by faith, not by doing the Law. The New Perspective (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright) stresses that first-century Judaism was a religion of grace and covenant, and that Paul's target is the use of Torah as a badge that keeps Gentiles out. The 'Paul within Judaism' school (Mark Nanos, Pamela Eisenbaum, Paula Fredriksen) goes further: Paul remained a Torah-observant Jew, and his letters address Gentiles about how they, as Gentiles, join Israel's God without becoming Jews. All three agree that Romans makes no sense unless it is read as a Jew's argument about Israel's Scriptures, Israel's Messiah and the destiny of Israel and the nations together.

flow.label: The gospel of God's Son
flow.detail: Paul introduces himself and the good news about the Davidic Messiah, now powerful to save the Jew first and also the Greek.

flow.label: Everyone under sin
flow.detail: Gentile idolatry and Jewish failure alike show that all humanity stands guilty before God; having the Law does not exempt anyone.

flow.label: God's righteousness in Christ
flow.detail: God has acted in Jesus' sacrificial death to put right all who trust, as Abraham trusted before circumcision.

flow.label: From Adam to Christ
flow.detail: Believers are at peace with God, freed from sin's reign, and joined to the risen Christ in baptism.

flow.label: Law, flesh and Spirit
flow.detail: The good Law could not overcome sin in the flesh, but the Spirit gives life, adoption and an unbreakable hope.

flow.label: Has God's word failed?
flow.detail: Paul wrestles with Israel's unbelief and insists God has not rejected his people; all Israel will be saved.

flow.label: One body, living sacrifices
flow.detail: Mercy creates a new way of life: renewed minds, mutual love, non-retaliation and respect for authorities.

flow.label: Welcome one another
flow.detail: Strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, must welcome each other as Christ welcomed them, so the church can support the mission to Spain.

mindmap.center: God's faithful righteousness in the Messiah

keyWords.meaning: Being in the right, and God's own faithfulness in putting things right. To 'justify' is to declare someone in the right, like a verdict in court, but in Romans it also means being counted part of God's covenant family. Traditional readers stress the legal verdict; New Perspective readers stress covenant membership; many hold both.

Trust, but also loyalty and reliability. 'The faith of Jesus Christ' (Rom 3:22) can mean faith in Christ or Christ's own faithfulness; scholars are divided. Paul pairs it with obedience in 'the obedience of faith' (Rom 1:5).

A gift from a benefactor. In ancient culture a gift created a relationship and expected gratitude. Paul's shock is that God gives to the unworthy, even enemies (Rom 5:6-10), which John Barclay calls the 'incongruity' of grace.

The same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the lid of the ark of the covenant where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Translators debate whether 'propitiation' (turning away wrath) or 'expiation' (removing sin) is closer; many now render it 'mercy seat' or 'place of atonement'.
Usually the Torah given to Israel at Sinai. Paul calls it holy, just and good (Rom 7:12), yet says it could not give life because of sin. Sometimes nomos means 'principle' or 'rule' (Rom 7:21-23).
Being made a son and heir. Paul applies it to believers by the Spirit and lists it first among Israel's privileges.

connections.how: Abraham is Paul's main test case: he was counted righteous by trusting God's promise before he was circumcised, so he is father of both Jewish and Gentile believers.
Paul's theme verse quotes Habakkuk's 'the righteous will live by faith(fulness)', written when Babylon threatened Judah and God's people had to trust him through crisis.
Isaiah supplies Paul's mission texts (beautiful feet of messengers), his remnant theology and his hope that a deliverer will come from Zion.
Paul reads Moses' words about the word being near, in your mouth and heart, as pointing to the message of faith in Christ.
Galatians is the heated first draft of themes Romans sets out calmly: Abraham, faith, Law, Spirit and the unity of Jew and Gentile.
Acts tells of the collection trip Romans anticipates, Paul's arrest in Jerusalem, and how he finally reached Rome, as a prisoner rather than a missionary passing through.

jesusLens: Jesus is presented as the Jewish Messiah, 'descended from David according to the flesh' and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection (Rom 1:3-4). He is the 'end' or 'goal' (telos) of the Law (Rom 10:4), the new Adam whose obedience undoes Adam's disobedience (Rom 5:18-19), and the servant of the circumcised who confirms the promises to the patriarchs so that Gentiles might glorify God (Rom 15:8-9). Christian readers have traditionally seen in Romans 3:25 the clearest statement of Christ's death as atoning sacrifice. Jewish readers, such as contributors to the Jewish Annotated New Testament, note that Paul's argument depends at every step on Israel's Scriptures and that Romans 11 refuses to write Israel out of God's future, which makes Romans an important text for Jewish-Christian dialogue.

misreadings.topic: Romans as a timeless manual of individual salvation, with chapters 9-11 as a detour
misreadings.popular: Romans is the Bible's systematic explanation of how a person gets saved: everyone has sinned (3:23), the wages of sin is death (6:23), Christ died for us (5:8), and whoever confesses and believes is saved (10:9-10). This 'Romans Road' is the heart of the letter. Chapters 9-11 deal with a separate topic, predestination or Israel, and chapters 12-16 are practical application.
misreadings.inContext: Krister Stendahl argued in 1963 and 1976 that the introspective Western conscience, shaped by Augustine and Luther, read its own guilt-questions into Paul, while Paul's real question was how Gentiles become part of God's people. N. T. Wright, James Dunn and Richard Hays add that chapters 9-11 are the climax: the whole letter asks whether God has been faithful to Israel and to his promise that Abraham's family would bless the nations. Chapters 14-15 show the practical aim: a Jewish-Gentile church eating together. Picking verses from across the letter to make a four-step tract is useful for evangelism but cuts the steps out of Paul's actual argument.
misreadings.defence: Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner and Simon Gathercole agree that Romans is about Jews and Gentiles and that 9-11 are integral. But they argue that Paul's answer to the Jew-Gentile question is precisely that every individual, Jew or Gentile, is a sinner who must be justified by faith apart from works (Rom 3:20-24, Rom 4:4-5). The 'Romans Road' does accurately summarise real Pauline teaching, and Romans 1-8 does address the universal human plight. Both sides agree the letter is bigger than a tract, and that personal salvation and the formation of one people belong together.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If Romans is only about my individual salvation, the church's unity across ethnic lines becomes optional. If it is only about ethnic unity, the personal call to repent and trust Christ fades. Paul holds both.

misreadings.topic: Romans 9: individual predestination or Israel's calling?
misreadings.popular: Romans 9 teaches that God chooses before birth which individuals will be saved and which will be lost, like Jacob and Esau, and that humans have no right to question this (Rom 9:13, Rom 9:20-21).
misreadings.inContext: Many interpreters, including James Dunn, N. T. Wright and Brian Abasciano, note that Paul is answering why most of Israel has not believed, and that his Old Testament examples (Jacob and Esau, Pharaoh, the potter in Jeremiah 18) are about nations and God's purposes in history. In Malachi, 'Jacob I loved, Esau I hated' refers to the peoples Israel and Edom. On this reading Romans 9 is about God's freedom to shape his covenant people and include Gentiles, and the chapter flows into 10-11, where Israel's hardening is partial and temporary and the door is open to all who call on the Lord (Rom 10:13).
misreadings.defence: John Piper (The Justification of God, 1983), Thomas Schreiner and Douglas Moo answer that Paul's problem is precisely why some individual Israelites believe and others do not (Rom 9:6-8), so individual salvation is in view; that Paul's language of 'vessels of mercy' prepared for glory (Rom 9:23) is about eternal destiny; and that corporate election still involves individuals. This is a real scholarly disagreement, not a popular error, and it runs along the Calvinist-Arminian line. The popular mistake is to read Romans 9 alone, without Romans 10-11's ending in mercy for all (Rom 11:32).
misreadings.whyItMatters: Both readings affect how Christians speak about Israel, assurance and God's character. Reading 9-11 as one unit protects against using Romans 9 to say God has finished with the Jewish people.

misreadings.topic: Romans 13 as a blank cheque for any government
misreadings.popular: Romans 13:1-7 means Christians must always obey the government because every authority is directly instituted by God; resisting the state is resisting God.
misreadings.inContext: The passage sits inside a section on love and not taking revenge (Rom 12:17-21, Rom 13:8-10). Paul is telling a small, vulnerable minority in the imperial capital, recently disrupted by the expulsion under Claudius and perhaps tempted to refuse taxes, not to give Rome a pretext for violence. Elsewhere Paul assumes rulers can crucify the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8), and Jewish tradition taught that God sets up kings yet judges them (Dan 2:21, Dan 4:17). Scholars such as Neil Elliott and Robert Jewett read the passage as pastoral caution, not a theory of the state.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical commentators such as Moo and Schreiner reply that Paul does state a general principle: authority as such comes from God and is meant to restrain evil. But they agree it is not unconditional. Acts shows apostles obeying God rather than men when commanded to stop preaching (Acts 5:29), and the mainstream Reformed tradition, from Calvin's remarks on lesser magistrates onwards, allowed for limits. Both sides reject using Romans 13 to silence protest against injustice.
misreadings.whyItMatters: This text was used to support both obedience to Nazi authorities and apartheid; reading it in context helps believers honour authority without giving it what belongs to God.

relevance.then: Roman believers learned that their divisions over food and days were not small matters: Jew and Gentile eating together was a sign that God had kept his promise. They were asked to see Paul's mission as theirs and to send him on to Spain with their support.
relevance.now: Romans still grounds Christian assurance (Rom 8:1, Rom 8:38-39) and shaped Augustine, Luther, Wesley and Barth. Read whole, it also asks churches divided by culture, class or politics to welcome each other, rejects Gentile arrogance toward the Jewish people, and ties personal faith to a shared mission.

sources.author: Douglas J. Moo
sources.title: The Letter to the Romans (NICNT, 2nd ed.)

sources.author: Peter Lampe
sources.title: From Paul to Valentinus: Christians at Rome in the First Two Centuries

oneLine: Paul tells a gifted, status-hungry church in a Roman boom town that the cross turns the world's ladder of honour upside down, and answers their questions about sex, food, worship and the resurrection in that light.

author.name: Paul, with Sosthenes
author.who: Paul founded the church in Corinth around 50-51 and stayed about eighteen months (Acts 18:11). Sosthenes may be the synagogue leader beaten in front of Gallio's tribunal (Acts 18:17), later a believer, though the name was common.
author.howWeKnow: Paul names himself, refers to his founding visit and closes in his own hand (1 Cor 16:21). Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth around 96, refers back to this letter by name (1 Clement 47). Authorship is undisputed.

writtenFrom.note: Paul says he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost (1 Cor 16:8) and sends greetings from the churches of Asia (1 Cor 16:19). He had already written an earlier letter that is now lost (1 Cor 5:9).

writtenTo.who: The church Paul founded in Corinth: mostly Gentile converts, a few Jews, a handful of better-off householders and many ordinary workers and slaves
writtenTo.situation: Members of Chloe's household reported factions (1 Cor 1:11), and Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus brought a letter of questions (1 Cor 7:1, 1 Cor 16:17). The church was splitting along lines of favourite teachers, social rank and spiritual giftedness, while tolerating sexual sin and taking each other to court.

worldEvents.event: Rome destroys the old Greek city of Corinth.
Julius Caesar refounds Corinth as a Roman colony, Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis, settled largely by freedmen.
Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca, serves as proconsul of Achaia (dated by an inscription found at Delphi); Paul is brought before him (Acts 18:12-17).
Isthmian Games are held near Corinth in alternate years (51 is one usually suggested while Paul was there), the background to Paul's runner and boxer images (1 Cor 9:24-27).
Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus; Nero becomes emperor in October.

backdrop:
The Corinth Paul knew was a young city. The old Greek Corinth had been destroyed by Rome in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 BC as a Roman colony, and many first settlers were freed slaves. By the 50s it was the capital of the province of Achaia and a booming trade hub on the narrow isthmus between two seas, with harbours at Lechaion and Cenchreae and a paved slipway (the diolkos) for dragging ships across. It was a place where people with money and ambition could climb quickly, and where public inscriptions advertised who had paid for what.

Archaeology shows that world. A paving stone near the theatre records that one Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for being made aedile, a city official. Many scholars identify him with the 'Erastus the city treasurer' of Romans 16:23, written from Corinth; others, notably Steven Friesen, question the identification and the first-century dating, so it is suggestive rather than proven. The Delphi inscription that names Gallio as proconsul lets historians date Paul's first stay around 50-51, one of the firmest dates in Paul's life.

The church reflected the city. 'Not many of you were wise by human standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth' (1 Cor 1:26) implies some were. Better-off members hosted the church and its meals, and the problems at the Lord's Supper, where some ate well while others went hungry (1 Cor 11:20-22), look like a Roman dinner party where guests were served according to rank. Members ranked teachers like celebrity orators (1 Cor 1:12, 1 Cor 3:4), went to civil courts where the wealthy usually won (1 Cor 6:1-8), and treated speaking in tongues as spiritual status. Paul's answer to all of it is the cross: God chose the shameful and weak to shame the wise and strong.

culture.explain: As a Roman colony Corinth ran its affairs in Latin with Roman-style magistrates, and freedmen could gain wealth and office there that was barred to them in Rome. Honour was earned in public through benefactions and recorded in stone. Paul's boasting only in the Lord cuts against this.

Greek cities prized polished public speakers (sophists) who charged fees and gathered fans. Paul deliberately refused to perform like them and worked with his hands instead of taking patronage (Acts 18:3), which some in Corinth saw as low-status.

At Roman dinners the host's friends reclined in the dining room with the best food while lesser guests ate elsewhere and later. When the church copied this, the meal meant to show one body in Christ became a display of class. Paul says this is not the Lord's Supper at all.

Most meat in the market had been offered to a god, and social life (guild meals, birthdays, civic feasts) happened in temple dining rooms; dining rooms have been excavated at Corinth's sanctuary of Asclepius. Refusing could cost a person business and friendships, which is why Paul gives a careful answer in three chapters.

Accepting money from a patron put you under obligation to them. Paul's refusal to accept support in Corinth kept him free from the powerful but offended those who wanted him as their client-teacher, an issue that flares again in 2 Corinthians.

In Roman society married women covered their heads in public as a sign of modesty, and men covering their heads was associated with leading pagan sacrifice. Paul's instructions are tangled up with these honour codes; how far they are cultural or permanent is debated.

jewishLens:
Although written to mostly Gentile converts, 1 Corinthians assumes that these former idol-worshippers have been brought into Israel's story. Paul calls the wilderness generation 'our fathers' (1 Cor 10:1) to Gentile readers, which means Israel's ancestors are now theirs too. He retells the exodus, the manna, the water from the rock and the golden calf as warnings for them (1 Cor 10:1-11). He calls Christ 'our Passover lamb' and tells them to clean out the old leaven, as a Jewish household did before Passover (1 Cor 5:7-8), and he plans his travels around Pentecost (1 Cor 16:8).

The ethics are Jewish ethics. Paul's ban on sexual immorality and idolatry echoes what Jews required of Gentiles who turned to Israel's God (compare Acts 15:20), and his reasoning about the church as God's temple (1 Cor 3:16-17) imports the Jerusalem temple's holiness into a Gentile congregation. Most striking, Paul quotes the Shema, Israel's confession that the LORD is one (Deut 6:4), and expands it: 'one God, the Father... and one Lord, Jesus Christ' (1 Cor 8:6). Richard Bauckham and N. T. Wright see this as placing Jesus within the identity of Israel's one God, without abandoning Jewish monotheism.

Paula Fredriksen and other 'Paul within Judaism' scholars point out that Paul never tells these Gentiles to become Jews, but he does insist they stop worshipping other gods, which was the one thing pagan society found offensive. 'Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God' (1 Cor 7:19) shows a Jew who still thinks God's commands matter, while denying that Gentiles must become Jews. And the resurrection hope of chapter 15 is a Pharisaic, Jewish hope in the raising of bodies, not the Greek hope of a soul escaping its body.

flow.label: Divided over leaders
flow.detail: Factions boast in Paul, Apollos or Cephas; Paul answers with the foolish wisdom of a crucified Messiah.

flow.label: Holiness in the body
flow.detail: Incest, lawsuits and prostitution are incompatible with being a people bought with a price and indwelt by the Spirit.

flow.label: Marriage and singleness
flow.detail: Answering their letter, Paul affirms marriage and sexual mutuality, and commends singleness for undivided devotion in a time of distress.

flow.label: Idol food and freedom
flow.detail: Knowledge puffs up but love builds up: give up rights for the weaker sibling, and never share in idol worship.

flow.label: Worship that builds up
flow.detail: Head coverings, the Lord's Supper and spiritual gifts must reflect one body where the weakest members are honoured.

flow.label: The more excellent way
flow.detail: Without love every gift is noise; in public worship intelligible speech that builds others up is better than tongues.

flow.label: Bodies will be raised
flow.detail: Christ's resurrection is the firstfruits; denying bodily resurrection empties the gospel.

flow.label: Collection and greetings
flow.detail: Practical plans for the Jerusalem gift and visits, ending with an Aramaic prayer: Maranatha, Our Lord, come.

mindmap.center: The cross reshapes a status-hungry church

keyWords.meaning: The word for a city's citizen assembly, and in the Greek Old Testament for the assembly of Israel. Paul's 'church of God that is in Corinth' (1 Cor 1:2) is God's assembly, a rival civic body with a different Lord.

Paul uses 'body' for the physical person (which matters to God and will be raised), for the bread of the Lord's Supper, and for the church as Christ's body, a common political image for a city whose members must cooperate.
Clever speech and philosophy prized by the elite. Paul contrasts it with 'the word of the cross', which looks like folly but is God's power and wisdom.
Charismata comes from charis, gift; the Corinthians spoke of pneumatika, 'spiritual things'. Paul insists they are given by the one Spirit for the common good, not as status markers.
Self-giving love that seeks another's good. Chapter 13 is not a wedding poem but a rebuke to a gifted, competitive church.

connections.how: Paul reads Israel's wilderness story as a warning to the church: same baptism-like crossing, same spiritual food, same danger of idolatry.
Paul's 'one God... one Lord' reworks the Shema, and his expulsion command quotes Deuteronomy's 'purge the evil from among you'.
Acts 18 tells of the church's founding with Priscilla and Aquila, the synagogue split, Crispus and Sosthenes, and Gallio's ruling.
The sequel shows how the relationship broke down further after this letter, and how the 'collection' Paul mentions here was later revived.
Paul's words over the bread and cup are closest to Luke's version of the Last Supper, suggesting a shared tradition.
Paul's closing hymn of victory over death draws on Isaiah's promise that God will swallow up death for ever.

jesusLens: For 1 Corinthians, Jesus is above all 'Christ crucified' (1 Cor 2:2), the Messiah whose shameful death exposes human wisdom and status. He is the one Lord through whom all things exist (1 Cor 8:6), the Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7), the rock that accompanied Israel in the wilderness (1 Cor 10:4) and the last Adam whose resurrection is the firstfruits of a new humanity (1 Cor 15:20-23, 1 Cor 15:45). The letter preserves the earliest written creed about his death, burial, resurrection and appearances (1 Cor 15:3-8), which most historians date to within a few years of the crucifixion. The Aramaic prayer 'Marana tha' (1 Cor 16:22) shows Jewish believers praying to Jesus as Lord in their own language very early.

misreadings.topic: 'You are God's temple' (1 Cor 3:16) as a verse about personal health
misreadings.popular: Your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, so you should not smoke, overeat or neglect exercise. 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 and 6:19 are taken together as teaching about looking after one's individual body.
misreadings.inContext: In 1 Cor 3:16-17 every 'you' is plural (Greek hymeis): 'you all are God's temple'. The context is factions over leaders. The 'temple' is the congregation, and destroying it means tearing the church apart through rivalry. Gordon Fee, Richard Hays and N. T. Wright stress that for a Jew the temple was the one place where God's presence dwelt among his people, so calling a Gentile house church God's temple is breathtaking. 1 Cor 6:19 does apply to individual bodies, but the issue there is sex with prostitutes, not diet: your body is joined to Christ and must not be joined to a prostitute.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars generally agree with this exegesis; Fee is himself a Pentecostal evangelical. They add that 6:19-20 really does teach that the individual body belongs to God and should be used to glorify him (1 Cor 6:20), so a careful application to stewardship of health is not wrong, provided it does not replace the main point. This is mostly a popular misunderstanding, not a scholarly dispute.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading 3:16 as about the community means church division is a sacrilege, a far stronger warning than most readers hear. It also keeps the sexual ethics of 6:19 from being reduced to general wellness.

misreadings.topic: 1 Corinthians 13 as a wedding reading about romantic love
misreadings.popular: 'Love is patient, love is kind' is a beautiful description of the love between husband and wife and is read at weddings for that reason.
misreadings.inContext: Chapter 13 sits between two chapters about spiritual gifts in worship. Its targets are the very failings of the Corinthian church: being puffed up (1 Cor 4:6, 1 Cor 8:1), seeking their own advantage (1 Cor 10:24), keeping records of wrongs (1 Cor 6:1-7). Paul is telling a competitive church that tongues, prophecy and knowledge without love are worthless. Scholars across traditions, such as Anthony Thiselton and David Garland, agree.
misreadings.defence: No serious scholar defends a purely romantic reading. Evangelical pastors note that the love described is the love Christ shows and applies to every relationship, marriage included, so reading it at a wedding is fine if the couple hears it as a costly, cross-shaped commitment rather than a feeling.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Heard in context, the chapter is a sharp challenge to churches that prize gifted performers over humble love.

misreadings.topic: Women silent in church (1 Cor 14:34-35) as a simple universal rule
misreadings.popular: Women must not speak in church services; Paul's command is clear and binding for all time.
misreadings.inContext: Three chapters earlier Paul assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in worship (1 Cor 11:5), so the command cannot mean total silence. Scholars propose different solutions: Gordon Fee and Philip Payne argue the verses are a later insertion because some manuscripts place them after verse 40; others (Craig Keener) think disruptive questioning by less-educated wives in a culture of honour is in view; others that Paul forbids women from publicly judging prophecies (1 Cor 14:29).
misreadings.defence: Complementarian scholars such as D. A. Carson and Wayne Grudem argue that the verses are original (they are in all manuscripts, only placed differently) and that Paul restricts women from the authoritative weighing of prophecy, a role tied to church leadership, rather than all speech. Egalitarian and complementarian scholars both reject the idea that women may never speak. The wider debate belongs to /debates/gender-roles.
misreadings.whyItMatters: How this text is read shapes women's participation in worship worldwide; seeing that 1 Cor 11:5 already assumes women speak narrows the real question.

relevance.then: A young church learned that being 'spiritual' meant serving the weak, that sexual and religious choices mattered because bodies belong to the Lord, and that the resurrection of the body was the heart of their hope.
relevance.now: Churches today face the same temptations: celebrity leaders, class divisions at the table, gifts used for show, freedom that ignores the conscience of others, and a vague spirituality without bodily resurrection. 1 Corinthians answers each one with the cross and the resurrection.

oneLine: Paul, hurt and accused of being weak, defends his ministry by showing that the gospel's power always comes through weakness, suffering and generous self-giving, just as it did in Christ.

author.name: Paul, with Timothy
author.who: Paul, the church's founder, now in a damaged relationship with it; Timothy had been his envoy to Corinth (1 Cor 4:17).
author.howWeKnow: The letter is full of personal detail that only Paul could give: his escape from Damascus in a basket (2 Cor 11:32-33), his vision of paradise (2 Cor 12:2-4), his 'thorn in the flesh'. Its authorship is not disputed; the debate is whether it is one letter or several.

writtenFrom.note: Paul says he went from Troas to Macedonia and met Titus there (2 Cor 2:12-13, 2 Cor 7:5-6), and he boasts to the Corinthians about Macedonian generosity (2 Cor 8:1-5, 2 Cor 9:2). Some late manuscripts add a note naming Philippi, but that is not original. If the letter combines several letters, parts may come from different places.

writtenTo.who: The church in Corinth and believers throughout Achaia
writtenTo.situation: Between 1 and 2 Corinthians Paul made a 'painful visit' (2 Cor 2:1) in which someone publicly insulted him, then wrote a 'tearful letter' (2 Cor 2:4). Titus brought news that most of the church had repented (2 Cor 7:6-13). But newcomers, whom Paul sarcastically calls 'super-apostles' (2 Cor 11:5), had arrived with letters of recommendation, impressive speaking and Jewish credentials, and they mocked Paul as weak in person and unprofessional for refusing pay.

worldEvents.event: Paul's 'painful visit' to Corinth and the 'tearful letter' (dates approximate).
Riot of the silversmiths in Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41); Paul may refer to deadly danger in Asia around this time (2 Cor 1:8-10).
Paul writes 2 Corinthians from Macedonia while gathering the collection.
Paul spends three months in Greece, presumably Corinth, and writes Romans (Acts 20:2-3), suggesting the reconciliation largely succeeded.

backdrop:
2 Corinthians comes out of a broken relationship. After 1 Corinthians, things got worse. Paul made a quick, painful visit; someone in the church wronged him publicly (2 Cor 2:5-8, 2 Cor 7:12); and he wrote a severe letter 'with many tears' that is probably lost. He changed his travel plans to avoid another painful visit and was then accused of being fickle (2 Cor 1:15-23). He nearly died in Asia, despairing even of life (2 Cor 1:8-9). When Titus finally met him in Macedonia with good news, Paul wrote with relief.

The letter's tone shifts sharply. Chapters 1-9 are warm and reconciling; chapters 10-13 are biting, ironic and defensive. Many scholars, including Margaret Thrall and Victor Furnish, think chapters 10-13 were a separate letter, possibly the tearful letter itself or a later one written after fresh bad news. Others, such as Murray Harris, David Garland and Ben Witherington, defend the letter's unity, explaining the shift as Paul turning from the repentant majority to the remaining opponents. Chapters 8 and 9 both address the collection and may also have been separate notes. The question does not change the letter's message, but it helps explain why it reads unevenly.

The rival teachers were Jewish believers ('Are they Hebrews? So am I', 2 Cor 11:22) who offered what Corinth admired: polished rhetoric, visions, letters of recommendation and a ministry that charged fees like a respectable teacher. Unlike the opponents in Galatia, they do not seem to have pushed circumcision. Paul's response is to boast, but to boast like a fool, listing beatings, shipwrecks, hunger and anxiety, and finally a humiliating escape over the wall of Damascus, the opposite of the Roman honour of being first over an enemy wall.

culture.explain: Travelling teachers carried letters from patrons vouching for them. Paul says the Corinthian church is his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts, echoing Jeremiah's new covenant.

A victorious general paraded through Rome with captives, incense burning along the route; some captives were led to execution. Paul pictures himself as a captive in God's triumphal procession, spreading the fragrance of Christ, a shocking image of apostleship as defeat that becomes victory.

Greco-Roman rhetoric allowed self-praise only under strict conditions and found it distasteful. Paul knows boasting is foolish but turns the convention inside out by boasting of his weaknesses, a technique scholars call a 'fool's speech'.
Cheap, fragile pottery lamps and storage jars were everywhere in Corinth, which had a large pottery industry. Treasure in clay jars means divine glory carried in breakable human bodies.

In the ancient world gifts created reciprocal bonds. Paul presents the collection for Jerusalem as charis (grace) that flows from God's gift in Christ, aiming at 'equality' (isotēs) between churches, not patron-client dependency.
Romans awarded a 'wall crown' to the first soldier over an enemy wall. Paul climaxes his list of credentials by being lowered down a wall in a basket to escape, a deliberate anti-boast.

jewishLens:
The heart of 2 Corinthians is a Jewish argument about covenants. In chapter 3 Paul compares his ministry with Moses'. He does not call the Sinai covenant evil: it came with glory so bright that Moses had to veil his face (Exod 34:29-35). But the new covenant promised by Jeremiah and Ezekiel, with the Spirit writing on hearts of flesh rather than tablets of stone (Jer 31:31-34, Ezek 36:26-27), has a greater and lasting glory (2 Cor 3:6-11). When Paul says a veil lies over the reading of Moses for many of his fellow Jews, he adds that 'when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed' (2 Cor 3:16), quoting Moses' own action of going in to speak with God.

This passage has often been read in an anti-Jewish way, as if Judaism were a religion of death. Scholars in dialogue with Jewish readers, including contributors to the Jewish Annotated New Testament and 'Paul within Judaism' writers, stress that Paul speaks as an insider making an intra-Jewish claim about the age of the Spirit, much as the Qumran community claimed to be the people of the new covenant. Traditional Reformed readers (Scott Hafemann, for example) emphasise that Paul does see a real contrast between the letter that kills and the Spirit who gives life, rooted in Israel's hard-heartedness in the wilderness, not in any defect of the Law itself.

Other Jewish threads run through the letter: God's comfort in suffering (Isa 40:1, echoed in 2 Cor 1:3-7), the new creation of Isaiah (Isa 43:18-19, Isa 65:17) behind 'the old has gone, the new has come' (2 Cor 5:17), and the collection for Jerusalem, which Paul treats almost like the pilgrimage of the nations bringing gifts to Zion (Isa 60:5). Even his opponents' claim to be 'Hebrews, Israelites, Abraham's offspring' shows that the debate was between Jews about what faithfulness to Israel's God now looks like.

flow.label: Comfort in affliction
flow.detail: Paul blesses the God of all comfort after near-death in Asia and explains why he changed his travel plans.

flow.label: Ministry of the new covenant
flow.detail: The Spirit's ministry outshines Moses'; believers are transformed into Christ's image from glory to glory.

flow.label: Treasure in clay jars
flow.detail: Suffering carries Jesus' death so that his life is seen; the outer self wastes away but hope looks to the unseen.

flow.label: Reconciliation and new creation
flow.detail: God reconciled the world to himself in Christ and appeals through Paul: be reconciled to God, and open your hearts to us.

flow.label: Grace of giving
flow.detail: The Macedonians' generosity and Christ's self-impoverishment ground an appeal to finish the collection for Jerusalem.

flow.label: Fool's boast
flow.detail: Against the super-apostles, Paul boasts of beatings, shipwrecks and a basket over a wall.

flow.label: Power in weakness
flow.detail: Visions aside, the thorn in the flesh taught Paul that Christ's grace is enough; he warns before a third visit.

mindmap.center: God's power made perfect in weakness

keyWords.meaning: Strength given alongside someone in distress. The word and its verb appear about ten times in 2 Cor 1:3-7 alone, setting the letter's tone.
The binding relationship God makes with his people. Paul contrasts the Sinai covenant on stone with the new covenant of the Spirit promised by the prophets.
A word from diplomacy and broken friendships: turning enemies into friends. Uniquely, Paul says the offended party, God, takes the initiative.
In chapters 8-9 charis means God's grace, the Macedonians' generosity and the collection itself; one gift flows into another.
Bodily frailty, low status and lack of impressive presence. For Paul it is where Christ's power rests.

connections.how: Moses' shining face and veil after Sinai are the basis of Paul's new-covenant argument.
The promise of a new covenant written on hearts lies behind 'letters written on hearts'.
Isaiah's 'new things' and 'day of salvation' are announced as arriving now.
The collection, Timothy's visit and the church's status-seeking all continue from the first letter.
Romans, written soon afterwards from Corinth, shows the collection was completed and the relationship restored.
The Macedonian churches praised here for giving out of poverty included Philippi, which also supported Paul personally.

jesusLens: In 2 Corinthians the pattern of Jesus' life becomes the pattern of ministry. 'Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor' (2 Cor 8:9); 'he was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God' (2 Cor 13:4). Believers see God's glory 'in the face of Jesus Christ' (2 Cor 4:6), language that recalls Moses seeing God's glory on Sinai. 2 Corinthians 5:21, 'him who knew no sin he made to be sin for us', is a key text for substitutionary atonement in Reformed theology; N. T. Wright reads its second half ('that we might become the righteousness of God') as about apostles embodying God's covenant faithfulness, a view others (Moo, Gathercole) dispute. All agree that Christ's death and resurrection are the template for how Christians, and especially leaders, are to live.

misreadings.topic: 2 Corinthians 9 as a promise of financial return for giving
misreadings.popular: 'Whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully' (2 Cor 9:6) means that if you give money (often to a ministry), God will multiply it back to you materially; giving is sowing a seed for your own harvest.
misreadings.inContext: Paul is raising famine relief for poor Jewish believers in Jerusalem. The harvest he promises is that God will supply enough so the givers can keep being generous ('so that you may abound in every good work', 2 Cor 9:8), that righteousness will grow, and that many will thank God (2 Cor 9:10-13). He quotes Psalm 112 about the generous person who scatters gifts to the poor. The aim is 'equality' between churches (2 Cor 8:13-15), echoing the manna in Exodus 16, where no one had too much or too little.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars such as Murray Harris and David Garland agree with this reading and strongly reject prosperity-gospel uses. They add, fairly, that Paul does promise that God will provide for generous givers' needs and reward generosity, so giving is never pure loss; the point is that the 'return' is sufficiency for further giving, not personal wealth. This is a popular misreading; there is little scholarly disagreement.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Read in context, the passage calls for cross-cultural generosity to the poor, not investment in one's own blessing.

misreadings.topic: 'New creation' (2 Cor 5:17) as only an individual's personal makeover
misreadings.popular: If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old personal habits are gone and the believer is a brand new person.
misreadings.inContext: The Greek is compressed: 'if anyone is in Christ, new creation!' Many scholars, including Richard Hays, J. Louis Martyn and Moyer Hubbard (who stresses the personal sense), discuss whether Paul means a new individual or the arrival of God's new world promised in Isaiah 65:17. The context is cosmic: God reconciling 'the world' (2 Cor 5:19), and a new way of knowing people 'not according to the flesh' (2 Cor 5:16). Believers belong to God's new creation already breaking into the old age.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars generally accept that both are present: the new world has begun in Christ, and the individual united to him really is changed. Hubbard argues the individual inner renewal is primary in this verse. The popular reading is not wrong, only too small.
misreadings.whyItMatters: If new creation is cosmic as well as personal, salvation includes how believers see others, cross social boundaries and hope for the renewal of all things.

relevance.then: The Corinthians were asked to stop judging leaders by charisma, credentials and eloquence and to recognise the crucified Messiah in a scarred, unimpressive apostle. They were also asked to keep their promise of giving to poor Jewish believers.
relevance.now: In an age of celebrity pastors, platform-building and image management, 2 Corinthians is a corrective: true ministry is accountable, unpaid by patrons where needed, open about weakness and marked by suffering love. It also offers deep comfort to people in chronic pain or failure: 'my grace is sufficient for you' (2 Cor 12:9).
